basis: way of life and way of death
note: The commentary's two forms of going are set against each other; the Didache opens by naming two ways and says their difference is great.

basis: two ways, of life and death
note: The Didache's opening contrast of the Way of Life and the Way of Death makes the commentary's two kinds of going into an early Christian ethical map.
The commentary presents dalal as a way whose destination is lost; the Didache specifies the way of death through the conduct that marks it.
The commentary's earth-disappearance question concerns whether the dead can be made new; Paul describes what is sown perishable being raised imperishable.
The commentary says the fabricated objects disappear from their adherents; Paul says an idol is nothing in the world, recasting their failure as the absence of a true divine power.

basis: an idol has no real being
note: Paul's claim that an idol has no real existence supplies a Christian conceptual counterpart to the commentary's false, fabricated objects proving absent rather than dependable.

basis: straying sheep returned to their shepherd
note: The readers were straying like sheep but have returned to the shepherd, a concise Christian movement from lost wandering to a responsible destination.

basis: turn from idols to serve the living God
note: The commentary says fabricated objects leave their worshippers; Paul describes converts turning from idols to serve the living and true God.
The commentary's people lost in earth ask about new creation; Paul says the dead in Christ rise at the Lord's descent.
The commentary's reply to disappearance is framed as meeting the Lord; Paul says the living and resurrected will be caught up to meet him.
God raises believers with Jesus and presents them together; resurrection is explicitly a movement into God's presence rather than a terminal vanishing.
The commentary gives a secondary sense of dalal as something vanishing from memory; Peter links short-sighted blindness with forgetting the cleansing from former sins.

basis: forsaking the straight way and going astray
note: The false teachers abandon the straight way and go astray, directly setting a right route against wandering in the terms the commentary contrasts.
The commentary says God neither loses nor forgets; Paul says the Lord knows those who are his, marking divine recognition as secure.
The commentary says a road has direction and destination; Paul's vision of a Macedonian asking for help redirects his travel toward a new destination.
The commentary says Joseph's disappearance leads into the road of travelers; Stephen's retelling continues with God delivering Joseph and making him ruler in Egypt.

basis: Joseph sold, yet God was with him
note: The commentary's Joseph vanishes from his brothers and passes into travelers' hands; Stephen retells the sale to Egypt while stressing that God was with Joseph.

basis: Joseph sold into Egypt, yet God with him
note: Stephen's retelling retains the brothers' sale of Joseph but adds that God was with him, explicitly reading the apparent loss as a providentially accompanied passage.

basis: Philip directed onto a desert road
note: The commentary describes a traveler on a route with a destination; an angel sends Philip onto the Jerusalem-to-Gaza road, where the encounter that follows leads to the eunuch's baptism.

basis: confidence to enter the holy places
note: The verse names entry into God's holy presence as the believers' goal, the arrival required to read the next verse's new and living way as more than a road metaphor.

basis: new and living way through the veil
note: Jesus inaugurates a new and living way through the veil; the Christian image joins a specifically living route to access before God.

basis: Red Sea crossed as dry land, Egyptians swallowed by it
note: Israel crosses the sea as dry ground while the Egyptians are swallowed when they attempt it, sharply contrasting water as a way of arrival with water as consuming loss.

basis: make straight paths so the lame may heal
note: The commentary requests a straight road; Hebrews urges straight paths for the feet so the impaired limb may be healed rather than further dislocated.

basis: make straight paths for your feet
note: The exhortation to make straight paths for the feet seeks restoration rather than dislocation for the lame, a pastoral Christian use of straight-path imagery.

basis: hearts go astray and do not know God's ways
note: Hebrews applies the wilderness generation's persistent going astray to its failure to know God's ways, directly coupling dalal-like error with an unrecognized divine route.
The divine oath that the straying generation will not enter God's rest supplies the destination denied to those who have not known God's ways.
No creature is unseen before God and all are exposed to him, supplying the divine-sight side of the commentary's assertion that nobody can be absent from judgment.

basis: God is not unjust to forget work
note: Hebrews explicitly denies that God forgets the readers' work and love, a direct theological counterpart to the commentary's negation of divine loss and forgetting.

basis: Jeremiah's promise applied to the new covenant
note: The commentary's claim that God does not lose or forget meets Hebrews' quotation of Jeremiah that God will remember sins no more; Hebrews frames that promise as the new covenant established through Jesus.

basis: God will no longer remember sins
note: Hebrews uses divine non-remembrance as covenantal forgiveness of sins, not as failed recall; that deliberate sense of "not remember" usefully distinguishes it from the commentary's claim that God never loses knowledge or forgets.

basis: walking in darkness without knowing where
note: The commentary uses dalal for one who goes where no one knows; Jesus warns that the one walking in darkness does not know where he is going.

basis: walking in darkness without knowing where one goes
note: Jesus says that the person walking in darkness does not know where he is going, an exact formulation of movement whose destination has vanished from knowledge.

basis: Jesus as way to the Father
note: Jesus identifies himself as the way by which one comes to the Father; it is a Christian construal of a road whose point is arrival before God.

basis: the dead hear and come out
note: The commentary's dead are hidden in earth; Jesus says all in the tombs will hear his voice.

basis: all in tombs hear the summons

The commentary's question concerns the destination after bodily disappearance; John distinguishes those who come out to life from those who come out to judgment.
Those in tombs come out for life or judgment, supplying both the new emergence and the accountable end that the commentary joins to earth-loss.
The commentary says the Lord does not lose or forget; Jesus tells the disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.
The commentary says the Lord does not lose or forget; Jesus says not one sparrow is forgotten before God.

basis: lost sheep found in the wilderness
note: The commentary uses dalal for someone whose whereabouts are unknown; Jesus' shepherd searches the wilderness until he finds the lost sheep.

basis: recognition and disappearance at the destination

basis: Isaiah's straight paths applied to John's mission

basis: Isaiah's road read as John's preparation

The commentary says the day gathers people and no one is absent; Jesus depicts all nations gathered before the Son of Man and separated for judgment.

The broad road leads to destruction, furnishing the adverse route and end alongside Matthew's life-leading way.
The commentary's sirat is a traversed way with an arrival; this verse makes the difficult way lead to life.
The restricted way leads to life and is found by few; it makes the endpoint of a path, rather than mere motion, decisive.

basis: the dead stand before the throne
note: The commentary says no one is absent from the Day of Judgment; Revelation pictures the dead, great and small, standing before the throne as books are opened.

basis: books opened for the dead's judgment
note: The dead stand before the throne and are judged from opened books, joining the commentary's book, non-forgetting, and no-one-absent motifs in one judgment scene.

basis: sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead
note: The sea, Death, and Hades yield their dead for judgment, a precise final-assize counter-image to persons or things apparently lost in earth or water.

basis: all stand before God's judgment seat
note: The commentary denies anyone can be absent from judgment; Paul says all will stand before God's judgment seat.
The commentary says no one escapes the Day of Judgment; Paul specifies that each person will give an account to God.
The commentary denies that anyone or anything is missing from judgment; Paul says God judges people's secrets through Jesus Christ.

basis: earth and Sheol return what was entrusted

basis: earth preserves and restores the dead

basis: the King of the world raises the dead
note: The martyred brother says that the King of the world will raise those who die for the law to everlasting life, a direct Jewish rebuttal to death as final loss.

basis: earth gives up those asleep in it
note: The commentary's dalal includes burial in earth; 4 Ezra pictures the earth restoring those who sleep in it at the judgment.

basis: earth and dust give up their sleepers
note: At judgment the earth gives up those asleep in it and dust those dwelling silently, an unusually close Jewish apocalyptic answer to people thought lost in earth.

basis: traveler asks for safe guidance and arrival

basis: God takes and will restore the soul

basis: pit containing no water but danger

basis: every deed written in a book

basis: from a drop to dust, then account before the King

basis: Joseph's waterless pit contains snakes and scorpions

basis: no escape through Sheol or heaven

The commentary says none can be absent from judgment; Amos says even captives among enemies remain within God's reach.

basis: written in the book and delivered

The commentary says none are absent on the Day of Judgment; Daniel sees the court sit and books opened, giving judgment an image of complete accounting.

basis: God goes ahead to find a campsite

basis: blind groping and failing on the way

basis: blind groping and failure in one's ways
note: The curse imagines groping at noon as a blind person in darkness and not succeeding in one's ways, combining impaired sight with failed direction.

basis: walk in God's way and live
note: The commentary asks for guidance along the path of those favored; Deuteronomy links walking in God's ways with life and blessing.

The commentary says the things idolaters fabricated disappear from them; Moses asks where the nations' gods are when their worshippers need refuge.

basis: fool cannot find the way to the city

The commentary's road has a destination; the Song of the Sea says God leads the redeemed people toward the dwelling of his holiness.

basis: guarded way to a prepared place
note: The commentary describes a traveler disappearing along a road that still has a destination; God sends a messenger to guard Israel on the way and bring them to the prepared place.

basis: guard on the way, brought to a place

basis: Moses asks to be blotted from the book

The commentary's lost person has gone where no one knows; Ezekiel pictures God searching for scattered sheep and rescuing them from the places where they were dispersed.

basis: seek the lost and bring back the strayed

basis: graves opened and people brought to their land

basis: led on the journey to a household

basis: kept on the journey and brought back
note: The commentary says a path may hide the traveler while still reaching its end; God promises Jacob presence wherever he goes and return to the land.

basis: Joseph cast into a wilderness pit
note: Reuben directs that Joseph be put into a pit in the wilderness rather than killed, giving the older narrative's concrete counterpart to Joseph's removal into the hidden bottom of a well.

basis: Joseph hidden in the dry pit
note: The commentary recalls Joseph disappearing into the pit before reaching a caravan; Genesis tells the same scene, with the pit empty of water.

basis: pulled from the pit into the traders' route
note: The commentary says Joseph's disappearance in the pit leads to the road and travelers; Genesis has passing traders draw him up and carry him into their journey.

basis: traders draw Joseph from the pit and take him to Egypt
note: Passing traders draw Joseph out and carry him toward Egypt, so the pit disappearance becomes a transit with an unforeseen destination, as the commentary emphasizes.
The commentary says Joseph's disappearance in the pit leads into a travelers' route; Genesis gives that route an Egyptian destination when Joseph is sold to Potiphar.

basis: Joseph interprets his journey as being sent ahead
note: The commentary reads the pit's disappearance as a route with an eventual destination; Joseph later says God sent him ahead to preserve life, interpreting that route as purposeful.

The commentary quotes those who ask whether people lost in earth can be created anew; Isaiah directly addresses the dead in dust and calls them to awake.

basis: voice says which way to walk

basis: "This is the way; walk in it"

basis: highway where travellers do not err
note: Isaiah's holy highway is specifically a way on which even wayfarers do not go astray, closely joining a directed road to the commentary's contrast between sirat and dalal.

basis: prepare a way in the wilderness
note: The commentary's sirat is a road that carries travelers toward an arrival; Isaiah calls for a way to be prepared in the wilderness for God's coming.

basis: make a straight highway for God
note: The wilderness proclamation makes a straight highway for God's coming; it supplies the road-and-arrival imagery behind a straight way without reducing the Qur'anic prayer to a lexical match.

basis: blind led on an unknown way
note: The commentary's blind people strive toward the path yet cannot see it; Isaiah promises that God will lead blind people on an unfamiliar way, turn darkness to light, and not abandon them.
God leads blind people on ways they have not known and turns darkness to light before them; this is the salvific reversal of the commentary's sightless people unable to find the path.
The commentary says a traveler may leave sight yet still be carried toward an arrival; Isaiah recalls God making a road through the sea for Israel's passage.
The commentary's path has direction and destination; Isaiah promises a new way in the wilderness and water in the desert, turning a trackless place into a route.

basis: idol worshippers cannot see or understand
note: The commentary depicts fabricated objects disappearing from their adherents; Isaiah says the idol-makers' eyes are shut and their hearts cannot understand.

basis: idol makers and witnesses are nothing
note: The commentary says fabricated objects vanish at the gathering; Isaiah calls the makers of idols nothing and their witnesses unable to see or know.
The commentary says the Lord neither loses nor forgets; Isaiah contrasts a mother who might forget with God's assurance that Zion will not be forgotten.

The commentary says God's knowledge does not lose what is entrusted to it; Isaiah intensifies the promise not to forget Zion by picturing her inscribed on God's hands.

basis: sea depths made into a way for the redeemed
note: God makes a way through the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross, a vivid counter-image in which water becomes a directed road rather than a place where things disappear.
The commentary's blind runners cannot see the path; Isaiah depicts people groping like the blind and stumbling even at noon.
The people grope like the blind and stumble at midday as in twilight, a direct image of vision failing to orient movement.

basis: they do not know the way of peace
note: The commentary's dalal is loss of direction; Isaiah says the people do not know the way of peace and have made their paths crooked.

The commentary places the loss of fabricated objects at judgment; Jeremiah says they perish when the time of their punishment comes.

basis: way of life and way of death
note: The commentary sets an arriving path against a lost way; Jeremiah explicitly places before the people a way of life and a way of death.

basis: God chooses not to remember forgiven sin
note: The commentary says the Lord neither loses nor forgets; Jeremiah's new-covenant promise says God will forgive and remember sin no more, distinguishing deliberate pardon from loss of knowledge.

basis: lost sheep led astray by shepherds
note: Jeremiah calls the people lost sheep whose shepherds led them astray across mountains; its failed guides give the commentary's dalal a communal and directional scene.
The commentary identifies a path with a direction and destination; Jeremiah tells the people to seek the good way, walk in it, and find rest.

basis: leaders wander in a pathless waste
note: The commentary contrasts a guided road with directionless disappearance; Job says God makes the leaders of the people wander in a trackless waste.

basis: God calls and the dead answer
note: The commentary connects disappearance in earth with eventual meeting; Job imagines God calling and the dead answering, giving the hoped-for return a personal encounter.

basis: God sees every human way and step
note: God's eyes are upon a person's ways and see every step, directly answering the commentary's difference between a traveller leaving human sight and nothing being lost to divine knowledge.
The commentary denies that anyone can vanish from judgment; Job says evildoers have no darkness or deep shadow where they can hide.

basis: water vanishes from its place in heat
note: Job's seasonal streams are scorched and disappear from their place; this is a textual water-loss image beside the commentary's example of something consumed and lost in water.

basis: caravans leave their course and perish
note: The same wadi scene has caravan routes turn aside into waste and perish, bringing the commentary's linked images of vanishing water and travellers without a destination into one scene.

basis: waters over the head and the cry "I am cut off"
note: The lamenter describes water closing over his head and concludes that he is cut off, a close scriptural scene of disappearance in water.

basis: calling God's name from the lowest pit
note: From the lowest pit the speaker calls on God by name, making the concealed pit a place from which relationship and appeal remain possible.

basis: God comes near to the pit-bound caller
